claims.claim: Native American cultures had a rich history of oral literature before European arrival; the written tradition in English is conventionally dated from the early 17th century, when English-speaking Europeans arrived in what became the United States.

Survey treatments conventionally divide American literature into five periods — Colonial and Early National (17th century to 1830), Romantic (1830 to 1870), Realism and Naturalism (1870 to 1910), Modernist (1910 to 1945), Contemporary (1945 to present) — with dates that vary by source (Writing the Nation dates its chapters Late Romanticism 1855-1870, Realism 1865-1890, Naturalism 1890-1914, Modernism 1914-1945, and post-1945).

Representative early-period examples include John Smith, whom Britannica identifies as writing some of the earliest works, and Phillis Wheatley, whom Britannica identifies as having written the first African American book.

The term 'American Renaissance' comes from F. O. Matthiessen's 1941 study and is conventionally applied to mid-19th-century writing by the Transcendentalists (Emerson, Thoreau) and by Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman; later scholarship notes that Matthiessen's catalogue neglected writing by women, African Americans, and Native Americans whose works were not widely recognized until the 1970s.

Realism (roughly 1865-1890) is represented by Mark Twain, Henry James, and Kate Chopin; naturalism (roughly 1890-1914) by Stephen Crane, Frank Norris, and Jack London; local color (1865-1885) and the more psychologically inward regionalism (1875-1895) are related sub-movements that render particular regions' dialect, customs, and settings.

Modernism (roughly 1914-1945) includes Robert Frost, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway, and Arthur Miller, alongside Harlem Renaissance writers Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, and Nella Larsen; post-1945 American literature includes Ralph Ellison, James Baldwin, and Toni Morrison, whom Britannica singles out for centering her works on the Black experience and receiving the Nobel Prize in 1993.

Recurring themes across periods include identity (including the new identities formed in the Harlem Renaissance), freedom of expression (emphasized in the Romantic-era account), the American dream (questioned in Fitzgerald's stories and Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman), and region (local color and regionalism).

Slave narratives such as Frederick Douglass's Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass form a distinct American autobiographical form that later writers such as Booker T. Washington adapted (in Up From Slavery).

A survey's period labels are generalizations for orientation; analyzing a particular text means arguing a debatable thesis with specific textual evidence (Purdue OWL) and examining what a text says and how it says it (OpenStax).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Period boundary dates differ between sources.
positions: Britannica: Colonial and Early National (17th century to 1830); Romantic (1830-1870); Realism and Naturalism (1870-1910); Modernist (1910-1945); Contemporary (1945-present).
Writing the Nation (open anthology): Late Romanticism (1855-1870); Realism (1865-1890); Naturalism (1890-1914); Modernism (1914-1945); American literature since 1945.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents dates as approximate conventions that overlap and vary by source, following the brief's instruction for a survey topic to name dates only as the sources give them.

positions: Matthiessen's 1941 The American Renaissance recognized significant mid-19th-century American (mostly New England male) writers.
Writing the Nation argues the term's catalogue neglected writing by women, African Americans, and Native Americans whose works were not widely recognized until the 1970s.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both: the label's conventional use and the scholarly critique, so students see the term as an interpretive claim rather than a neutral fact.
